Here's what *Poison* does in Frosthaven, straight from the rulebook:

> **Poison:** All attacks targeting the figure gain "+1 Attack." Poison is removed when the figure is healed but, unlike *Wound*/*Brittle*/*Bane*, poison prevents the heal from increasing the figure's current hit point value.

- **Offensive debuff:** Every attack made against a *Poisoned* figure gets +1 to its attack value.
- **No turn-based expiration:** Unlike conditions such as *Muddle* or *Stun*, *Poison* does **not** wear off at the end of a turn — it persists until the figure is healed.
- **Healing removes it, but blocks HP recovery:** When a *Poisoned* figure is healed, the *Poison* token is removed, but the hit point increase from that heal is **prevented**. The heal is still "used up" — it just cleanses the condition instead of restoring HP.

*(Rulebook, passage 101)*

Here's how looting works in Frosthaven:

---

## The *Loot* Ability

> "*Loot* X" is an ability that allows a figure to loot all loot tokens and treasure tiles within range X, including any in their current hex. This ability is unaffected by the presence of figures or overlay tiles. If there are no loot tokens or treasure tiles within the specified range, the ability cannot be performed.

*(Rulebook, passage 111)*

---

## Looting Loot Tokens

When a loot token is looted, it is **removed from the map**:
- **Monsters:** Nothing else happens.
- **Characters:** Draw one card from the **loot deck** (unless it's empty).

The four types of loot cards are:
- 💰 **Money** — coins converted to gold based on scenario level (gained at end of scenario).
- 🪵 **Material Resources** (lumber, metal, hide) — varying amounts based on party size (gained at end of scenario).
- 🌿 **Herb Resources** (arrowvine, axenut, corpsecap, flamefruit, rockroot, snowthistle) — one herb each (gained at end of scenario).
- 🎲 **Random Item** — the character immediately draws from the random item deck and adds it to their item pool. They may use it for the rest of the scenario even if it puts them over the item limit. If the random item deck is empty, it counts as a money card with three coins. This can only be gained **once per scenario**.

---

## Looting Treasure Tiles

When a treasure tile is looted, it is **removed from the map**. **Monsters cannot loot treasure tiles.** If it's a numbered treasure, look it up in the Treasure Index and apply the effect — only the looting character gains the reward (unless it's a random item blueprint or random scenario).

---

## Key Reminder

Money and resources are **not gained until the end of the scenario**, but random items are gained **immediately** when looted.

*(Rulebook, passages 111–112 and passage 67)*

> At recommended difficulty, the scenario level is equal to the average level of the characters divided by 2 (rounded up).

Here's how *advantage* works with attack modifier cards in Frosthaven:

---

## Advantage — Drawing Two Modifiers

When an attack has *advantage*, the attacker **draws two modifier cards** and uses one of them:
- A **monster** always uses the **better** one.
- A **character** may use **either** one.

---

## Rolling Modifiers with Advantage

If the **first draw** is a *rolling modifier*, the process changes:
1. Keep drawing additional modifiers one at a time until a **non-rolling modifier** is drawn.
2. Then draw **one more** modifier, ignoring any rolling icon on it.
3. The attacker uses **all the initial rolling modifiers** plus **whichever of the last two they choose**.

If the **first draw is not** a rolling modifier but the **second draw is**, the rolling icon on the second card is still **ignored**.

---

## Ambiguity

When it's unclear which modifier is "better" or "worse" (e.g., elemental infusions or negative conditions), **the attacker must use the one drawn first**. Any non-numeric effect is considered to have a positive but undefined value.

---

## Advantage + Disadvantage Cancel Out

> "An attack cannot gain multiple instances of advantage or disadvantage. If an attack has both advantage and disadvantage, it is considered to have neither."

---

## Ranged Attack on Adjacent Enemy

Any **ranged attack targeting an adjacent enemy** automatically gains *disadvantage*.

Here is a full summary of **Looting** in Gloomhaven (2nd Edition), based on the rulebook:

---

## Loot Ability

> **"Loot X"** is an ability that allows a figure to loot all money tokens and treasure tiles within range X, including any in their current hex. This ability is unaffected by the presence of figures or overlay tiles. If there are no money tokens or treasure tiles within the specified range, the ability cannot be performed.

*(Rulebook, passage 132)*

---

## End-of-Turn Looting

> Characters must loot any money tokens or treasure tiles present in their hex **at the end of their turn**. No figures besides characters perform end-of-turn looting.

- Note: this happens at the **end of the full turn**, not at the end of each individual movement.
- Monsters and summons do **not** perform end-of-turn looting.

*(Rulebook, passages 156 & 290)*

---

## What Happens When Something Is Looted

**Money tokens:**
- Removed from the map when looted.
- If looted by a **monster**, nothing else happens (the token is simply removed).
- If looted by a **character**, they place the token on their character mat.

**Treasure tiles:**
- Removed from the map when looted.
- **Monsters cannot loot treasure tiles.**
- If it is a **numbered treasure**, the character references the Treasure Index and applies the effect. Only the looting character gains the reward, unless it is a random item design or random scenario.
- If a character gains a duplicate item they already own, they must give it to another character or sell it immediately.

*(Rulebook, passage 133)*

---

## Monster Loot Abilities

Some monsters have explicit loot abilities on their ability cards. In those cases:
- The monster loots all **money tokens** within the specified range, removing them from the map.
- Those money tokens are **not** dropped again when the monster dies.
- Monsters with loot abilities still **cannot** loot treasure tiles.

*(Rulebook, passage 182)*

Here's how the recommended scenario level is calculated in **Gloomhaven (2nd Edition)**:

> At recommended difficulty, the scenario level is equal to the average level of the characters **divided by 2** (rounded up).

**Formula:** `Average Character Level ÷ 2 (rounded up)`

**Example:** If all characters are level 2, the average (2) ÷ 2 = 1, so the scenario is still level 1. Only once a character reaches level 3 would the scenario level potentially increase to 2.

---

### Adjusting Difficulty

- You can set the scenario level to **any value from 0–7** at the start of a scenario, regardless of the recommended level.
- **Solo mode** (one player controlling two or more characters): Add 1 to the average character level *before* dividing by 2 and rounding up. Formula: `((Average Character Level + 1) ÷ 2, rounded up)`
- **Open Information variant**: Use the same calculation as solo mode.

Here's how *Advantage* works with attack modifier cards in **Gloomhaven (2nd Edition)**:

---

## Advantage

> With **advantage**, the attacker draws two modifiers and uses one of them. A monster always uses the better one, but a character may use either one.

---

## Rolling Modifiers with Advantage

Things get a bit more involved when rolling modifiers appear:

> If the first draw with advantage or disadvantage is a rolling modifier, the attacker draws additional modifiers, one at a time, until a non-rolling modifier is drawn. **They then draw one more modifier and ignore any rolling icon on it.**

> The first non-rolling modifier and the one after it are compared. If the attack has advantage, the attacker uses all initial rolling modifiers and whichever of the last two modifiers they choose.

**In plain terms:**
1. Keep drawing as long as you're hitting rolling modifiers.
2. Once you hit the first non-rolling card, draw **one more** (treating it as non-rolling even if it has a rolling icon).
3. You apply all the rolling modifiers you accumulated, then **choose** which of the final two non-rolling modifiers to use.

---

## Example (from the rulebook)

The attack has *Advantage*, and the first card drawn has a rolling icon (e.g., a "Self" effect). Since it's rolling, a second card is drawn — it also has a rolling icon (+0). A third card is drawn (+1, also with a rolling icon, but it's the final draw so the rolling icon is ignored). The player uses **all the rolling modifier effects** plus the **+1** card (their choice of the last two).

---

**Source:** Gloomhaven (2nd Edition) Rulebook, passage 103 (Advantage and Disadvantage section).

> **Can I skip targets in a red hex AoE attack?** Yes; a red hex AoE just determines the hexes where your potential targets are. Note - this is a change from the Gloomhaven 1e FAQ, and is to make it consistent with all other non-mandatory targeting.

A few important notes from the same FAQ section:

- **Targeting is non-mandatory** — red hexes define *potential* targets, not *required* targets. You choose which figures within those hexes to actually attack.
- **Line of sight is still required** — you must have line of sight to any figure you choose to target.

- **This is a rules change from 1e** — in Gloomhaven 1st Edition, red hex AoE attacks were mandatory (you had to hit all valid targets). That is **no longer the case** in 2nd Edition.
